title: QUERY INSIGHTS HUB
summary: Researchers had learned to work around a slow, overloaded query hub. I turned 18 findings into 4 V1 priorities; observed query creation moved from 5–10 minutes to under 2 minutes, and the final design was implemented for the research team.

children: Engineering constraints shaped the system, but they were not the UX problem.
The expert heuristic audit surfaced 18 design findings across hierarchy, system feedback, query construction & recovery.
I prioritized 4 failures: buried work states, competing controls, a system-led builder & memory-dependent work.
The challenge: preserve the complexity experts needed while removing the complexity the interface created.

children: Each priority maps a legacy failure to its task consequence & V1 response.
Surface failures, drafts, progress & new-query confirmation.
Keep essentials visible; move secondary controls into More Filters.
Start with query logic; show nested hierarchy, live SQL & inline validation.
Support Frequent/Recent values, duplication, copying & drafts.
4 decisions shaped V1 across attention, hierarchy, query construction & recovery.
Kept essential filters visible and moved secondary controls into More Filters or contextual actions.
Surface failures, drafts, progress & new-query confirmation.
Brought failed queries, drafts, indexing progress & newly created work out of the table.
Make query logic the primary task
Opened on the builder, preserved nested AND/OR hierarchy & moved secondary details into the next stage.
Added Frequent/Recent values, duplication, copying & drafts so recurring logic did not need to be rebuilt.

I explored two directions across the saved-query table, query builder, creation flow, and system feedback. After reviewing both with the Product Owner, I combined selected elements into V1 and deferred lower-priority requirements to later releases.

attrs.alt: First pass: move the query up. Changing field order did not separate competing decisions. Schematic reconstruction.
Four ways to organize the builder. What stays in view, what can be reused, and what can wait.
What did each builder layout solve? Keep logic and feedback visible; delay details that do not help construction.
Builder context stayed visible. Reuse & secondary work waited until needed.

children: “I combined feedback from two directions into a focused V1: 4 interaction priorities guided what remained in scope, while lower-priority requirements were sequenced across V1.1–V1.3.”
Kept secondary filters, columns, and bulk actions available only when relevant.
Kept query identity, logic, selection, and system state visible throughout the task.
Added contextual validation, query previews, and recovery near the point of failure.
Used searchable controls, reusable queries, and sensible defaults without removing advanced functionality.
I designed and implemented the workflow around:
Observed task checks across varied old and redesigned UI tasks showed query creation move from 5–10 minutes to under 2 minutes on average.
Engineering implementation used pagination, debouncing, lazy-loading & virtualization to support the designed workflow. These technical results were evaluated separately from the UX outcome.
This project demonstrates end-to-end ownership across product design and frontend implementation. Formal usability testing and adoption measurement remain future work.
